The expansion includes support for background tasks, allowing agents to process work asynchronously without blocking user interactions, and integration with remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for extended functionality. Managed Agents abstract away the complexity of building agentic systems from scratch — developers can focus on defining what they want their agents to do rather than engineering the orchestration layer themselves. The background tasks feature is particularly important for real-world applications where agents need to handle long-running operations like data processing, file generation, or external API calls without timing out or freezing the user experience. MCP integration opens the door for agents to connect to specialized tools and data sources beyond what's built into the API, making them far more versatile for enterprise use cases. This positions Gemini API's Managed Agents as a more complete alternative to custom-built agent frameworks, reducing development time and operational overhead for teams building AI-powered applications.

Instead of treating indexing and model serving as separate systems, SilverTorch treats the index itself as the model, eliminating redundancy and bottlenecks that plague traditional recommendation pipelines. The results are dramatic: SilverTorch achieves up to 23.7x higher throughput compared to state-of-the-art approaches, while also delivering 20.9x better compute cost efficiency versus CPU-based solutions. Critically, these efficiency gains don't come at the expense of accuracy—SilverTorch actually improves recommendation quality alongside the performance improvements. This matters enormously for platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and Threads, where milliseconds of latency and infrastructure costs directly impact user experience and operational budgets. The research paper details how consolidating the retrieval layer reduces data movement, memory overhead, and computational waste. For companies running recommendation systems at scale—particularly social platforms, content aggregators, and e-commerce sites—SilverTorch represents a significant step forward in making high-quality personalization economically viable.

articles.hook: Meta just solved the problem that breaks every privacy system.
articles.headline: Meta's Data Classification Framework: The Missing Piece for AI Privacy Controls
articles.body: Meta Engineering has released a comprehensive approach to privacy-aware infrastructure built specifically for the AI-native era, addressing a fundamental challenge that has plagued data governance systems: accurately identifying and classifying data before privacy controls can operate on it. The core insight is deceptively simple but powerful — privacy controls like retention policies, access restrictions, purpose limitations, and anonymization rules cannot function without knowing exactly what data they're protecting. The problem is more complex than it appears. Consider a field labeled 'age': in one database it might represent a customer's birth year (personally identifiable information requiring strict protection), in another it could be an anonymized age bracket for analytics (lower sensitivity), and in a third it might be derived from facial recognition output with different legal implications entirely. Meta's framework, documented as an asset classification case study, provides systematic methods for disambiguating such contexts before data flows through AI systems. This matters urgently because AI companies are rapidly scaling data processing — the infrastructure that worked for traditional databases breaks down when millions of data flows need real-time governance. Without reliable classification, companies either over-restrict data (killing legitimate ML use cases) or under-restrict it (creating compliance and privacy risks). Meta's approach gives teams concrete patterns for building privacy controls that actually scale with AI workloads, particularly relevant for organizations training large models or running inference pipelines on sensitive data. The framework is being released as open guidance, making it immediately applicable to any company operating privacy-critical AI infrastructure.
examples: Tag ambiguous fields by their source and context, then apply purpose-specific retention rules automatically.
Block downstream model sharing when data crosses legal jurisdictions or consent boundaries.
Anonymize sensitive features before ML training while preserving signal for legitimate use cases.

The engineering challenge lies in computing these signals in real-time across Meta's infrastructure while keeping latency low enough for seamless scrolling. The feature represents a shift back toward social-first discovery after years of algorithm-dominant feeds, potentially giving individual friend networks more influence over what content reaches you.

articles.hook: Google just brought together the people who'll shape AI in schools.
articles.headline: Google Convenes 150 Education Leaders to Map AI's Classroom Future
articles.body: Google, in partnership with the New York Jobs CEO Council and Urban Assembly, hosted an AI summit at its New York offices bringing together 150 education and industry leaders to collaborate on integrating artificial intelligence into classrooms. The summit represents a significant effort to align business, policy, and educational expertise around how AI tools should be deployed in schools. Rather than a product announcement, this was a strategic convening designed to shape the conversation around responsible AI adoption in education—covering topics like teacher training, curriculum design, student outcomes, and equitable access. The gathering underscores Google's broader push to position itself as a responsible player in the education space while influencing how AI implementation happens at scale. For educators and entrepreneurs, this signals growing institutional support for AI-powered learning tools, but also indicates that adoption will require coordination between tech companies, school systems, and city-level policy makers. No specific AI tools or models were announced, but the summit creates a roadmap for how companies can work with schools to deploy AI responsibly.

articles.hook: Meta just hit a decade of backing Python. Here's why that matters.
articles.headline: Meta Marks 10 Years Supporting Python—Here's Why Open Source Matters
articles.body: Meta announced it has completed its 10th consecutive year as a sponsor of the Python Software Foundation (PSF), the nonprofit organization responsible for advancing, supporting, and protecting Python—one of the world's most influential and widely-used programming languages. Python powers everything from data science and machine learning to backend infrastructure and AI development, making PSF sponsorship a strategic bet on the entire ecosystem that underpins modern AI engineering. Meta uses Python extensively across its entire engineering stack, from research to production systems, meaning the company has a direct incentive in Python's health and evolution. The PSF relies on corporate sponsorships and donations to fund community initiatives, security improvements, documentation, and developer education globally. By maintaining decade-long consistent support, Meta signals serious commitment to the open-source infrastructure that its own AI and engineering teams depend on. This kind of foundational investment in programming language communities is how companies ensure the tools they use remain maintained, secure, and aligned with industry needs.
examples: Engineers build AI models and data pipelines in Python, reducing development time from months to weeks.
